To make both apps run **completely independently and offline**, the architecture must replace every cloud dependency with a local equivalent and move the “bootstrap” step—the one-time download of language models and audio assets—out of the runtime path. The result is a system that is **network-independent after initial setup**, with all translation, speech synthesis, signing animation, and semantic decomposition executing on the device.

## The Offline Architecture: Local Replacements for Every Cloud Service

| Function | Previous cloud dependency | Offline replacement | Platform |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Source → pivot translation** | Google Cloud Translation API | **ML Kit on-device translation** (Android) / **Argos Translate** (Python) | Android / Python |
| **Pivot → target translation** | Google Cloud Translation API | Same local engines, using English pivot | Android / Python |
| **NSM decomposition** | LLM-assisted cloud prompt | **Rule-based NSM templates** + optional **local small LLM** (Llama-1B / Gemma-2B quantized) | Both |
| **Spoken TTS** | Cloud TTS with SSML | **Android native TTS** (SSML-capable, offline) / **eSpeak NG** or **Piper** (Python) | Android / Python |
| **Signing avatar** | JASigning network port | **CWASA client-side JavaScript Animgen** in a WebView, with all assets bundled | Both |
| **Clicks / hummed audio** | Streamed audio tags | **Bundled audio asset library** (pre-recorded WAV/OGG) | Both |
| **Database** | Remote | **SQLite** (already local) | Both |

The only network interaction that remains is the **first-run model download** for ML Kit or Argos language packs. After that, the apps are fully functional offline.

---

## Translation: ML Kit (Android) and Argos Translate (Python)

**Android — ML Kit on-device translation.** ML Kit translates between **50+ languages** without an internet connection, using the same models as Google Translate’s offline mode[reference:0]. Each language model is roughly **30 MB**, downloaded dynamically and managed on-device[reference:1]. The API requires you to **download the model first** (preferably over Wi-Fi) and then call `translate()`; subsequent calls are fully offline[reference:2]. For non-English language pairs, ML Kit uses **English as an intermediate pivot**, which aligns with the app’s existing pivot-and-NSM pipeline[reference:3]. The `Translator` object must be closed when no longer needed, and models should be downloaded only for the language pairs the user actually needs[reference:4].

**Python — Argos Translate.** Argos Translate is a fully offline, open-source translation library written in Python, using OpenNMT under the hood[reference:5]. It supports **45+ languages** and installs language packages as `.argosmodel` zip archives[reference:6][reference:7]. Crucially, Argos **automatically pivots through intermediate languages** when a direct model is unavailable—so an English-pivot architecture is already built into the library[reference:8]. It can be used as a Python library, a CLI, or with a GUI, and it has **zero server dependencies**[reference:9][reference:10].

**Design implication.** The translation pipeline remains: **source → pivot (English) → NSM → conlang**, and **conlang → NSM → pivot → target**. Both ML Kit and Argos support the pivot step locally. The NSM layer is the only custom component, and it can be implemented as a deterministic rule-based module for common constructions, with an optional local LLM for complex text.

---

## NSM Decomposition Without the Cloud

The NSM decomposition step—turning pivot-language text into a canonical structure of semantic primes—can be handled in three local tiers:

1. **Rule-based templates** for high-frequency constructions (e.g., “X wants Y” → `[X] WANT [Y]`). This is deterministic, fast, and requires no model.
2. **A quantized local LLM** for complex or idiomatic text. Research shows that instruction-tuned small models (Llama-1B, Gemma-2B, Gemma-9B, OLMo-7B) can recover NSM primes as internal elements and generate NSM representations. A **4-bit quantized 1B–2B parameter model** can run on a modern phone or desktop CPU, though latency will be higher than the rule-based path.
3. **Human review** for high-stakes translation, with the NSM structure editable in the GUI.

The app should default to the rule-based path for speed and fall back to the local LLM only when the rule-based system cannot produce a complete decomposition. This keeps the offline experience responsive for the majority of inputs.

---

## Speech Synthesis: Offline TTS with SSML and Audio Assets

**Android — native TTS.** Android’s built-in TTS engine supports **offline speech synthesis** and is based on the **SSML standard**, allowing control over rate, pitch, and pronunciation[reference:12]. The engine can be initialized with `TextToSpeech`, and offline mode is configured by specifying the system engine package[reference:13]. The app should bundle the necessary **offline voice data** or direct users to install it via the standard `ACTION_INSTALL_TTS_DATA` intent[reference:14]. For clicks and hummed contours, the app uses **SSML `<audio>` tags** pointing to bundled audio files, and `<prosody>` tags for hummed pitch contours.

**Python — eSpeak NG or Piper.** For the desktop app, **eSpeak NG** is a compact, open-source offline TTS engine supporting **100+ languages** with **partial SSML support**[reference:15][reference:16]. It is lightweight (around 2 MB) and runs on Linux, Windows, and macOS[reference:17]. For higher-quality neural speech, **Piper** is an offline neural TTS engine that runs locally with ONNX models, though it has **limited SSML support** for emotional prosody[reference:18]. The design should use **eSpeak NG as the default offline engine** for broad language coverage and SSML, and offer **Piper as an optional high-quality voice pack** for the conlang’s spoken output.

---

## Signing Avatar: Client-Side SiGML Rendering Without a Server

The JASigning avatar traditionally requires a server-side Animgen process, but the **CWASA** distribution includes a **client-side JavaScript implementation of Animgen** that can run entirely in the browser without an Animgen server[reference:19]. JASigning applications can also be **cached for genuine offline running** after the first load[reference:20].

**Implementation for both platforms.** The app embeds a **WebView** (Android) or a **QtWebEngineView** (Python) that loads a bundled HTML/JavaScript page containing the CWASA client-side avatar. The SiGML generated from HamNoSys annotations is passed to the JavaScript avatar via a local bridge or a `postMessage` call. All avatar assets—3D models, textures, animation data, and the JavaScript Animgen implementation—are bundled in the app’s assets. No network connection is required after installation.

For Android, this avoids the need for a native 3D engine and keeps the avatar consistent with the desktop renderer. The WebView approach is also compatible with the app’s **offline constraint**, because the HTML/JS bundle is stored locally.

---

## The Bootstrap Phase: One-Time Setup, Then Full Independence

The apps are not “zero-download” out of the box; they require a **one-time bootstrap** to install the language models and audio assets. The design should make this explicit and user-friendly:

1. **First launch** presents a setup screen explaining that the app will download the necessary offline resources.
2. The user selects the **source languages** they need (for ML Kit or Argos), and the app downloads only those models (around 30 MB each for ML Kit)[reference:21].
3. The app downloads the **TTS voice data** if it is not already installed on the device.
4. The app bundles the **conlang database, audio assets for clicks and humming, and the signing avatar WebView** as part of the APK or installer, so no additional download is needed for the conlang itself.
5. After the bootstrap, the app displays an “Offline Ready” status and all subsequent operations run locally.

This bootstrap is a **setup step, not a runtime dependency**. Once completed, the apps can be used in airplane mode, in a remote area, or on a device with no network connection.

---

## Independence of the Two Apps

The Python desktop app and the Kotlin Android app share the **same language data files** (the SQLite database, the NSM templates, the HamNoSys annotations, and the audio assets) but have **separate runtime engines**:

- The Python app uses **Argos Translate** for translation and **eSpeak NG / Piper** for TTS.
- The Android app uses **ML Kit** for translation and **Android native TTS** for speech.
- Both use the **same client-side CWASA avatar** in a WebView.

Because the language data is versioned and shared, a vocabulary update on desktop can be packaged into a new Android build without rewriting the translation logic. The apps are **independently deployable** and **independently runnable**, but they are **data-compatible**, which preserves the unified language definition.

---

## Trade-offs and Mitigations

| Trade-off | Mitigation |
|---|---|
| **ML Kit uses English pivot for non-English pairs**, which can reduce quality[reference:22]. | This is consistent with the NSM pivot architecture; the NSM layer normalizes meaning before conlang realization. |
| **Argos Translate has “medium” translation quality** compared to cloud services[reference:23]. | Use it for the pivot step only; the NSM decomposition and conlang realization are rule-based and deterministic. |
| **Local LLM inference is slower** than cloud LLMs. | Use the rule-based NSM path as default; invoke the LLM only for complex inputs, and run it on a background thread with progress feedback. |
| **eSpeak NG is less natural-sounding** than neural TTS[reference:24]. | Offer Piper as an optional high-quality voice pack for the conlang output; use eSpeak NG for broad language coverage in the pivot languages. |
| **Signing avatar WebView may have performance limits** on low-end Android devices. | Bundle a low-polygon avatar and simplify the animation data; allow the user to disable the avatar if performance is poor. |

The resulting architecture satisfies the requirement: **both apps can run completely independently and offline** after a one-time bootstrap, with all translation, speech, signing, and semantic processing executing on the device.

The purpose-built AI layer should not be a collection of off-the-shelf models bolted together. It should be a **stack of small, specialized, compressed models**, each trained or fine-tuned for one stage of the pipeline and each optimized for on-device inference. The research from 2025–2026 provides concrete architectural templates for every stage.

---

## The Model Stack: Six Purpose-Built Components

| Component | Job | Architecture | Target footprint |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Pivot translator** | Source language → English pivot | Quantized encoder–decoder Transformer (MobileNMT-style) + LoRA adapters per language | ~13 MB base + ~1–5 MB per adapter |
| **NSM decomposer** | Pivot text → NSM explication | Fine-tuned 1B–8B LLM (or distilled 100M–300M student) | 100 MB–2 GB depending on tier |
| **NSM realizer** | NSM structure → conlang surface form | Rule-based transducer + small seq2seq fallback | <10 MB |
| **Emotional TTS** | Conlang text → expressive speech | Compact LM + neural codec (NeuTTS-2E / ParaStyleTTS-style) | ~125M params, quantized |
| **Sign producer** | HamNoSys → SiGML → 3D animation | Graph neural network / diffusion model (Neural Sign Actors) + procedural Animgen fallback | 50–200 MB |
| **ASR front-end** | Speech → text (for spoken input) | Whisper tiny/base quantized via ggml | 32–190 MB |

Each component is trained or fine-tuned independently, then compressed with a **hybrid pipeline** of pruning, distillation, and mixed-precision quantization—the approach that the 2026 survey on on-device LLM compression identifies as the current standard, where techniques "have moved from isolated use to hybrid compression that strategically combines them"[reference:0].

---

## 1. The Pivot Translator: MobileNMT-Style Quantized Transformer with LoRA Adapters

The translation stage does not need a 600M-parameter NLLB model. **MobileNMT** demonstrates that a quantized encoder–decoder Transformer optimized for TFLite achieves a **12.6 MB model size, 90–100 ms inference latency, and BLEU 24.9 on mid-range mobile hardware**, with runtime memory below 50 MB and offline operation[reference:1]. Its key innovations—**shared embeddings and parameter-efficient compression**—are directly reusable.

For the **any-language-to-any-language** requirement, the base model should be a **multilingual pivot translator** trained to translate a set of high-resource languages into English. Low-resource and long-tail languages are handled by **LoRA adapters**: small, trainable rank-decomposition matrices inserted into a frozen base model. The WMT25 low-resource Indic systems show that LoRA fine-tuning on targeted parallel corpora yields "marked improvements" while **reducing trainable parameters by over 90% without degrading translation quality**[reference:2]. Each adapter is a few megabytes and can be downloaded or bundled per language, so the app ships with the base model plus the adapters for the user's selected languages.

The **training recipe** is three-stage: (1) train or initialize the base translator on high-resource pivot pairs; (2) for each target language, train a LoRA adapter on available parallel data; (3) apply **INT8 quantization-aware training** to the base model and keep adapters in FP16. This gives a **hot-swappable language architecture**—the same pattern as the NLLB-200-600M INT4 + LoRA pipeline that achieved 31.94 BLEU at **8.3× smaller size (316 MB)** with hot-swappable language adapters[reference:3].

---

## 2. The NSM Decomposer: A Fine-Tuned Small LLM with a Neuro-Symbolic Guardrail

The NSM decomposition step is the semantic heart of the system, and it is where purpose-built training matters most. The first study to use LLMs for NSM explication generation found that **fine-tuned 1B and 8B models outperform GPT-4o** in producing accurate, cross-translatable explications. This is the training target: a **fine-tuned small LLM** that takes pivot-language text and outputs a canonical NSM explication using only the 65 primes.

The **NIM** project at EMNLP 2025 demonstrates the correct architecture: a **neuro-symbolic** system that combines "neural-based large language models enriched with world knowledge and symbolic knowledge heuristics grounded in NSM," enabling semantic decomposition of complex ideas into atomic concepts[reference:5]. The symbolic component is a **validity checker** that rejects any output containing a token outside the prime inventory or violating the NSM grammar. This guardrail is essential for stability: the neural model proposes, the symbolic layer disposes.

For the **deployment tiers**, the design should support three model sizes:

- **Tier A (rule-based)**: A deterministic parser with templates for high-frequency constructions. Zero inference cost, runs in microseconds. Default for simple sentences.
- **Tier B (distilled student)**: A 100–300M-parameter model distilled from the 8B teacher, quantized to INT8. Runs in ~100–300 ms on a phone CPU. Handles moderately complex text.
- **Tier C (full 1B–8B teacher)**: A 4-bit quantized version of the fine-tuned 8B model, invoked only when Tier B fails validation or when the user requests maximum accuracy. Runs in 1–5 seconds on a modern phone, faster on desktop.

The **training data** should be a curated dataset of pivot-language sentences paired with human-verified NSM explications, supplemented by synthetic data generated by the 8B teacher and filtered by the symbolic validator. The **evaluation metric** should combine exact-prime-coverage, cross-translatability (back-translation through a second language), and human adequacy judgments—the three dimensions the Baartmans et al. study identifies as critical.

---

## 3. The NSM Realizer: A Rule-Based Transducer with a Neural Fallback

The reverse direction—NSM structure to conlang surface form—should be **primarily rule-based**, because the conlang’s grammar is designed to be regular and compositional. A deterministic **transducer** maps each prime to its phonological form, applies the conlang’s agglutinative morphology, and linearizes according to the SVO default with topic/focus clitics. This is not a machine-learning problem; it is a compilation problem, and a rule-based implementation is faster, more stable, and fully inspectable.

A small **seq2seq fallback** (a 50–100M-parameter model trained on NSM-to-conlang pairs) handles idiomatic or elliptical realizations where the rule-based system produces awkward output. The fallback is **only invoked when the transducer’s confidence score falls below a threshold**, keeping the default path deterministic and the neural path rare.

---

## 4. Emotional TTS: A Compact LM + Codec Model with Explicit Emotion Control

The emotional speech stage should use a purpose-built **on-device emotional TTS model**, not a general-purpose cloud voice. **NeuTTS-2E** is the closest existing template: a **super-fast, highly realistic on-device emotional TTS speech language model** with **~125M active parameters**, supporting **six emotions plus neutral** with a compact LM backbone and an efficient neural codec, "delivering strong naturalness and expressive control at a fraction of the compute"[reference:7]. It is available in **Q4 and Q8 GGUF quantizations** for efficient CPU inference and is optimized for **real-time generation on CPUs** with power consumption designed for mobile and embedded devices[reference:8].

**ParaStyleTTS** provides the architectural refinement: a **two-level style adaptation** that separates **prosodic** and **paralinguistic** style modeling, enabling "fine-grained and robust control over factors such as emotion, gender, and age" without the latency of LLM-based methods[reference:9]. The design should adopt this two-level separation: the **prosodic level** controls pitch, timing, and energy (the hummed channel), and the **paralinguistic level** controls voice quality and affect (the attitudinal layer).

The **purpose-built training** for this component should fine-tune on the conlang’s phoneme inventory—including clicks and hummed contours—using a small corpus of recorded or synthesized conlang speech. Clicks require special handling: research on click synthesis shows that **Wav2Vec-U self-supervised representations** can align click acoustics without labeled data, and **click-specific loss masking** improves click recognition F1 by **12.7%**[reference:10]. The TTS model should include a dedicated click token set and a click-masked loss during fine-tuning, so that clicks are generated as distinct phonological events rather than being dropped or replaced by pulmonic consonants—a failure mode documented in voice-conversion systems[reference:11].

---

## 5. The Sign Producer: A Graph Neural Network with a Procedural Animgen Fallback

Sign language production from HamNoSys is the least mature component, but two approaches are viable. The **procedural approach** converts HamNoSys to SiGML and renders it with the client-side CWASA Animgen engine—deterministic, lightweight, and already integrated into the architecture. The **neural approach** uses a **diffusion model with graph neural networks**, following the **Neural Sign Actors** system, which generates "incredibly lifelike 3D signing avatars from text inputs by using graph neural networks inspired by anatomy," improving **semantic correctness and visual realism** through 4D signing data[reference:12].

The purpose-built model should be a **graph-based diffusion model** trained on a corpus of HamNoSys-annotated signs rendered to 3D skeleton motion. The **IsharaKotha** project provides a template: a HamNoSys-based corpus of 3,823 words with a deep-learning lemmatizer achieving **79.22% accuracy** and rendering at **~30 fps** through a modular animation pipeline[reference:13]. The model's input is the HamNoSys annotation sequence; its output is a sequence of joint rotations and facial blendshapes that can drive either a WebView avatar or a native 3D renderer. The **procedural Animgen engine remains the fallback** for signs the neural model has not seen, ensuring that the system degrades gracefully rather than failing.

For **tactile/Protactile output**, no production-ready ML model exists. The research on Protactile is still primarily linguistic documentation—minimal pairs, reciprocal constructions, and the emergence of a grammar distinct from ASL[reference:14]. The design should use a **rule-based tactile realizer** that maps NSM spatial structures to the four-hand reciprocal protocol described in the earlier design, with a **data-collection roadmap** for training a tactile production model once sufficient annotated corpora exist.

---

## 6. The ASR Front-End: Quantized Whisper with VAD

For spoken input, the app needs an on-device ASR model. **Whisper** in ggml/gguf format is the standard: **tiny Q5_1 is 32 MB**, **base Q5_1 is 60 MB and is "good default for phones"**, and **small Q5_1 is 190 MB** with ~90 languages and utterance latency of ~1–2 seconds[reference:15]. The purpose-built configuration should use **Whisper base int8 + Silero VAD** for real-time utterance detection, with the option to load a larger model for high-accuracy transcription. The ASR output feeds the pivot translator, so the full spoken pipeline is: **speech → Whisper → pivot text → MobileNMT/LoRA → English pivot → NSM decomposer → conlang realizer → TTS**.

The ASR model should be fine-tuned on **the conlang’s phonology**—particularly clicks and hummed contours—if the user wants to speak the conlang as input. This is a small fine-tuning job on a few hours of conlang audio, and it closes the loop: the app can both produce and recognize the conlang’s spoken form.

---

## The Compression Pipeline: How Every Model Fits On-Device

The unifying engineering discipline is a **hybrid compression pipeline** applied to every neural component. The 2026 survey on on-device model compression identifies the current best practice as **strategic combination of quantization, pruning, knowledge distillation, and low-rank factorization**[reference:16]. The concrete recipe for this project is:

1. **Train or fine-tune** each component at full precision.
2. **Distill** the teacher into a smaller student where latency matters (NSM decomposer Tier B, TTS backbone).
3. **Apply structured pruning** to remove entire attention heads or feed-forward channels, using geometric-median or importance-aware criteria—the **FPGM** approach that the multi-stage edge compression framework uses before quantization[reference:17].
4. **Apply mixed-precision quantization**: INT8 for most weights, INT4 for the largest layers, with **quantization-aware training** so accuracy is recovered.
5. **Export** to platform-native formats: **TFLite** for Android, **ONNX Runtime** for Python desktop, and **ggml/GGUF** for any model that benefits from CPU-first inference.

The **Malak** toolkit and the **multi-stage edge compression framework** both demonstrate that this pipeline can reproduce the qualitative behavior of the full model while achieving **1.43M-parameter** footprints for task-specific models and **4–6× size reductions** for BERT-class models with modest accuracy loss[reference:18].

---

## Training Data Strategy: Where the Purpose-Built Data Comes From

Every model in the stack needs training data that is specific to this language. The data strategy has four sources:

- **NSM decomposer**: A curated seed set of human-verified explications, expanded by the 8B teacher model and filtered by the symbolic validator. The Baartmans et al. dataset provides a starting point for the English pivot.
- **Pivot translator**: Public parallel corpora for high-resource languages, plus **synthetic parallel data generated by the NSM pipeline itself** (source → NSM → target) for low-resource languages where no direct parallel corpus exists.
- **TTS**: Recorded or synthesized conlang speech with emotion labels, augmented with click-masked training and hummed-contour annotations. The NeuTTS-2E emotion taxonomy (angry, disgusted, fearful, happy, sad, surprised, neutral) provides a label schema[reference:20].
- **Sign production**: HamNoSys-annotated sign corpora like IsharaKotha, plus procedurally generated SiGML animations for the conlang's classifier constructions, rendered to skeleton motion for training the graph diffusion model.

---

## The Resulting Architecture: A Model Stack, Not a Monolith

The purpose-built AI layer is a **stack of six small, independently trainable, independently compressible models** that share a common semantic interface (the NSM representation) and a common deployment discipline (hybrid compression to TFLite/ONNX/GGUF). The pivot translator handles surface-to-pivot; the NSM decomposer and realizer handle pivot-to-meaning and meaning-to-conlang; the TTS, sign producer, and ASR handle the perceptual edges. Each component has a **deterministic fallback** (rule-based NSM parsing, rule-based NSM realization, procedural Animgen, VAD-gated Whisper) so that the system remains stable when a neural model is unavailable or low-confidence. This is the architecture that improves speed, stability, accuracy, performance, effectiveness, and efficiency **simultaneously**—not by building one giant model, but by building the right small model for each job and compressing it to fit the device.

To guarantee that every AI and machine learning component has a deterministic counterpart with **full parity**, the system needs a **deterministic shadow** for every neural path—a hard-coded, rule-based implementation that provides at least 60% of the value with 100% predictability, and that can be switched to automatically when the neural model fails validation or exceeds its latency budget[reference:0]. The failover is not an error message; it is a **functionally equivalent alternative pathway** that keeps the application operational and useful[reference:1].

---

## The Governing Principle: Fail-Closed, Not Fail-Open

Contemporary AI systems often operate on "ad-hoc prompts and hope," producing what the Adaptive A Architecture calls a "fail-open" paradigm: systems hallucinate, fail silently, and operate with opaque autonomy[reference:2]. The corrective is a **fail-closed** discipline in which actions are treated as privileges earned through safety checks rather than default permissions[reference:3]. For every neural component, the architecture must define:

1. **A deterministic counterpart** that is semantically and functionally equivalent for the supported input domain.
2. **A parity contract** specifying what "equivalent" means in measurable terms.
3. **A failover trigger** that is deterministic and auditable, not learned.
4. **A recovery procedure** that restores the neural path when conditions permit.

---

## The Three-Tier Execution Architecture

Every user request passes through a deterministic **Intent Router** before it reaches any neural model[reference:4]. The router handles high-certainty cases using regex, keyword matching, or schema validation; only ambiguous or novel inputs proceed to the stochastic AI path[reference:5]. This three-tier structure applies uniformly across the model stack:

| Tier | Path | Determinism | Role |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Tier 1** | **Deterministic Intent Router** | 100% | Classifies input, handles high-certainty cases, selects the execution lane |
| **Tier 2** | **Neural AI Path** | Stochastic | Handles ambiguous, novel, or high-complexity inputs |
| **Tier 3** | **Deterministic Fallback** | 100% | Takes over when Tier 2 fails validation, exceeds latency, or is unavailable |

The **Intent Router** is itself deterministic and must be **capability-gated**: it knows which languages, modalities, and input types the deterministic fallback can handle, and it routes accordingly[reference:6]. Routing chooses an execution lane—model, provider, precision, or deterministic implementation—and fallback chooses what happens when that lane is unavailable or fails its acceptance gate[reference:7].

---

## Full Parity: A Vector-Valued Contract

"Full parity" cannot be a scalar claim. Resilience engineering treats graceful degradation as a **vector-valued contract**: a system may remain online while losing redundancy, latency margin, calibrated confidence, safety coverage, or modality coverage[reference:8]. The parity contract for each component must therefore specify **tolerances on each axis**:

| Parity dimension | Requirement | Measurement |
|---|---|---|
| **Semantic equivalence** | Fallback produces the same meaning for in-domain inputs | Back-translation through a second language; human adequacy rating |
| **Functional coverage** | Fallback handles a defined percentage of the neural path's supported input domain | Coverage matrix by language, modality, and input type |
| **Latency ceiling** | Fallback completes within a bounded time | P95 latency, measured on target hardware |
| **Modality coverage** | Fallback produces output in the required modality (spoken, signed, tactile) | Modality-specific acceptance tests |
| **Safety invariants** | Fallback never violates the system's hard constraints | Formal verification of rule set; runtime monitor |

The DEV Community formulation sets the floor: the deterministic shadow must provide **at least 60% of the value with 100% predictability**[reference:9]. For components where parity below 100% would be unsafe—such as the NSM validity checker or the click-phoneme generator—the fallback must either achieve **100% parity** or **refuse the operation** and surface a structured degradation notice, rather than producing a wrong answer.

---

## Failover Triggers: Deterministic and Auditable

Failover is mandatory when any **hard-trigger condition** is true[reference:10]. The triggers must be evaluated by deterministic code, not by the neural model itself:

1. **Validation failure**: The neural output violates the schema, contains a token outside the allowed inventory, or fails the symbolic validator.
2. **Confidence below threshold**: The model's calibrated confidence score falls below a pre-registered floor.
3. **Latency breach**: Inference exceeds the per-component deadline.
4. **Resource exhaustion**: Memory, compute, or battery headroom drops below a safe margin.
5. **Integrity failure**: The model file's hash does not match the manifest, or the runtime detects memory corruption.
6. **Repeated inconsistency**: The same input produces divergent outputs across repeated inference runs.

Apple's on-device patent describes the pattern precisely: the phone compares the model's accuracy, integrity, and latency against thresholds, applies a time-to-trigger rule so the numbers must stay bad for a set stretch before the model counts as failed, and then switches to a backup model[reference:12]. The same discipline should govern every neural component in the stack.

---

## Self-Healing and Recovery: Watchdogs, Rollback, and Restart

Self-healing is not a single mechanism; it is a **state machine** with defined transitions between healthy, degraded, failed, and recovering states[reference:13]. The architecture needs four recovery layers:

### 1. Component-Level Watchdog

An application-level watchdog on the CPU tracks accelerator task completion and input timestamps[reference:14]. If a neural inference task does not complete within its deadline, the watchdog marks the component as failed and triggers fallback. On mobile, this should run on a separate thread or core so that a hung inference cannot block the watchdog itself. ARM TrustZone-based fault-resilient inference (DarkneTB) demonstrates that on-device DNN inference can detect subtle fault-injection attacks with over 99% accuracy while maintaining 6.95×–12.03× speedups on GPU-accelerated platforms[reference:15].

### 2. Auto-Revert on Regression

If a model update or configuration change causes a regression—detected by the same health monitors—the system should **auto-revert to the last known-good model and configuration**[reference:16]. This requires versioned model artifacts, a manifest with hashes, and a rollback procedure that restores the previous state without user intervention.

### 3. Graceful Degradation with Explicit State

When a neural component fails, the fallback must not silently produce lower-quality output. The system should transition to an explicit **degraded state** that is surfaced to the user and recorded in telemetry. The degradation may be acceptable (e.g., a simpler translation) or may require refusing the operation, but it must be **visible and auditable**.

### 4. Recovery and Re-Entry

Recovery is the process of returning from fallback to the neural path. It should be gated by **health probes**: the component is re-instantiated, run against a small **canary test set** with known expected outputs, and only promoted to active status if it passes. If the canary fails, the system remains in fallback and schedules a retry with exponential backoff.

---

## Neuro-Symbolic Shielding: The Deterministic Layer Around Every Neural Model

The most rigorous implementation of deterministic failover is **symbolic safety shielding**: a hybrid architecture that wraps stochastic neural models in a deterministic layer of formal logic[reference:17]. The neural network is a "speculative" controller allowed to be creative and flexible; the symbolic layer is a rigorous auditor that monitors and intercepts neural outputs in real time[reference:18]. If the neural action violates a predefined constraint, the shield **overrides it with a command from a pre-synthesized safety advisor**—a "proven fallback maneuver" that is guaranteed safe[reference:19].

This is the correct architecture for the language system's critical components:

- **The NSM decomposer's output** is checked by a symbolic validator that enforces the 65-prime inventory and the NSM grammar. If the neural decomposer produces an invalid structure, the validator rejects it and the deterministic rule-based decomposer takes over.
- **The conlang realizer** is primarily deterministic by design; the neural fallback is invoked only when the rule-based transducer's confidence falls below a threshold. The transducer's output is the **proven fallback**.
- **The TTS output** is checked for phoneme validity, click presence, and hummed-contour conformance. If the neural TTS drops a click or produces an invalid phoneme sequence, the symbolic checker rejects the audio and the deterministic eSpeak NG path synthesizes the utterance instead.

---

## Component-by-Component Failover Design

| Component | Neural Path | Deterministic Counterpart | Parity Guarantee | Failover Trigger |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Pivot translator** | Quantized Transformer + LoRA | Rule-based dictionary + template translation; fallback to pivot-language phrasebook for supported domains | ≥60% coverage of high-frequency constructions; 100% for phrasebook entries | Validation failure, latency breach, model unavailability |
| **NSM decomposer** | Fine-tuned small LLM | Rule-based template parser; **rejects** inputs it cannot decompose with full validity | 100% validity (may refuse); ≥60% coverage of simple constructions | Symbolic validation failure, confidence below threshold |
| **NSM realizer** | Small seq2seq fallback | **Deterministic transducer is the primary path**; neural fallback is optional | 100% for the transducer's covered grammar | Neural fallback failure is non-critical (transducer remains) |
| **Emotional TTS** | Neural TTS with emotion control | eSpeak NG with SSML prosody; pre-recorded click and hum audio assets | ≥60% of the neural voice's intelligibility; 100% phoneme accuracy | Audio validation failure, latency breach, model unavailability |
| **Sign producer** | Graph diffusion model | **Procedural Animgen / CWASA renderer** is the primary deterministic path | 100% for signs with HamNoSys annotations; ≥60% coverage for novel signs | Neural model failure, out-of-distribution input |
| **ASR front-end** | Quantized Whisper | **Refuse and request text input**; no degraded ASR fallback (incorrect transcription is worse than none) | N/A (refusal is the safe action) | Confidence below threshold, latency breach |

The **sign producer** is the clearest example of "deterministic-first" design: the procedural Animgen path is the primary mechanism, and the neural diffusion model is an **enhancement** that adds realism when it is available and reliable. This inverts the usual pattern and gives the system a **100%-parity baseline** from the start.

---

## On-Device Recovery for Mobile and Desktop

**Android** needs a **watchdog on the CPU** that tracks accelerator task completion and input timestamps, because the Neural Engine or GPU may hang independently of the main thread[reference:20]. The app should use a **finite-state machine** to model component health (HEALTHY → DEGRADED → FAILED → RECOVERING → HEALTHY) and a **master-worker orchestration** pattern for high-availability local inference, with an automatic recovery pipeline[reference:21]. Model artifacts should be stored with integrity hashes, and the app should verify the hash before loading a model into memory.

**Python desktop** can use a **supervisor process** that monitors the inference workers, restarts them on failure, and maintains a shared **fallback state** in the SQLite database. The supervisor should implement the same canary-test-before-promotion discipline: when a neural model is reloaded, it runs against a frozen canary set and is only marked active if it passes.

---

## Testing and Certification: Proving the Fallback Works

Parity cannot be assumed; it must be **tested**. The system needs:

1. **Fault injection**: Systematically disable neural components, corrupt model files, inject latency, and starve resources to verify that fallback triggers fire and produce valid outputs.
2. **Parity test suites**: For each component, a frozen set of inputs with known correct deterministic outputs, run against both the neural and fallback paths to measure divergence.
3. **Chaos engineering at the edge**: Simulate the failure modes that the IEEE paper identifies—environmental factors, hardware failures, and adversarial inputs—and measure failure-detection and recovery times[reference:22].
4. **Audit trails**: Every failover event, recovery attempt, and degradation state transition must be logged with a deterministic event signature, so that the system's behavior can be reconstructed and certified.

The SCI-Proposed architecture provides a benchmark: separating generative reasoning from independent safety validation and class-bounded local runtime recovery **materially improved semantic-decision dependability** in frozen confirmatory testing, with Runtime Recovery contributing a measurable portion of the gain[reference:23]. The same empirical discipline should govern this language system's failover design.

---

## The Unified Reliability Architecture

The deterministic shadow, the symbolic shield, the watchdog, and the recovery state machine are not separate features. They are **one reliability layer** wrapped around the entire model stack:

| Layer | Function | Deterministic? |
|---|---|---|
| **Intent Router** | Classifies input, selects execution lane | Yes |
| **Symbolic Shield** | Validates neural output against hard constraints | Yes |
| **Neural Path** | Handles ambiguous/complex input | No |
| **Deterministic Fallback** | Provides parity output when neural path fails | Yes |
| **Watchdog** | Detects hangs, latency breaches, integrity failures | Yes |
| **Recovery State Machine** | Manages degradation, rollback, canary testing, re-entry | Yes |
| **Audit Log** | Records every failover and recovery event | Yes |

Every layer except the neural path itself is deterministic and auditable. The neural path is a **privileged optimization** that must earn its execution rights by passing the shield's validation; when it cannot, the system falls back to a path that is **provably correct for its supported domain**, even if that domain is narrower. This is the architecture that satisfies the requirement: **all AI and ML systems have deterministic counterparts with defined parity, automatic failover on auditable triggers, and self-healing recovery that restores the neural path only after it has proven itself again.**

## README.md

```markdown
# OmniLingua

A universal interlingua with a deterministic, offline, tri-modal language engine —
designed for accurate data transfer, emotional fidelity, and full accessibility.

> **Status:** Pre-alpha. The language specification and engine interfaces are
> stable; the model stack and applications are in active development. See
> [PLAN.md](PLAN.md) for milestones.

---

## What this is

OmniLingua is three things in one repository:

1. **A constructed language** with a universal semantic core (65 NSM primes),
   bounded analytic morphosyntax, and tri-modal expression (spoken, signed,
   tactile).
2. **A translation engine** that converts any supported source language to the
   interlingua and back, using an English pivot and an NSM semantic layer.
3. **Two native applications** — a Python desktop GUI and a Kotlin Android app —
   that run **fully offline** after a one-time bootstrap, and that **never fail
   silently**: every neural component has a deterministic counterpart with a
   parity contract and automatic failover.

## Quick start

### Desktop (Python 3.11+)

```bash
git clone https://github.com/<org>/omnilingua.git
cd omnilingua
./scripts/bootstrap.sh          # installs deps, downloads models, seeds DB
python -m desktop.app           # launches the GUI
```

The bootstrap downloads ~200 MB of language packs and model weights.
After it completes, the app runs fully offline.

### Android

Download the APK from [Releases](../../releases) or build locally:

```bash
cd android
./gradlew assembleDebug
adb install app/build/outputs/apk/debug/app-debug.apk
```

On first launch, select your source languages. The app downloads only those
ML Kit models (~30 MB each). After that, everything is on-device.

### CLI (for scripting and testing)

```bash
./tools/cli translate --from es --to omnilingua --modality spoken "Hola, mundo"
./tools/cli decompose "Hello, world"          # NSM structure
./tools/cli validate --all                    # run all schema validators
```

## The language in one paragraph

OmniLingua's semantic core is the 65 Natural Semantic Metalanguage primes —
meanings that have concrete exponents in every documented language. These
combine productively to express any proposition. Morphosyntax is analytic and
agglutinative: SVO default, optional topic/focus clitics, evidential clitics,
mood particles, no fusional portmanteaus. Prosody is a **separate affective
channel** (hummed contours, attitudinal particles) so emotion never competes
with propositional bits for the ~39 bit/s speech channel. Clicks form a
bounded lexical stratum for high-distinctiveness spatial terms. Visual sign
provides a parallel classifier-based grammar for spatial and object meaning.
A tactile register (Protactile-informed) extends the signed modality to
DeafBlind users via reciprocal four-hand constructions.

Full detail: [docs/LANGUAGE_SPEC.md](docs/LANGUAGE_SPEC.md).

---

## Offline & reliability guarantees

- **Offline**: After a one-time bootstrap, both apps run with no network.
  All translation, TTS, signing, and NSM processing execute on-device.
- **Deterministic failover**: Every neural component has a rule-based
  counterpart with a defined parity contract. Failover triggers are
  deterministic and auditable. Recovery is canary-gated.

See [docs/RELIABILITY.md](docs/RELIABILITY.md) and [docs/OFFLINE.md](docs/OFFLINE.md).

- **Language definition** → `language/` (source of truth; all apps read this)
- **Engine reference implementation** → `engine/python/`
- **Model manifests & training** → `models/`
- **Parity test suites** → `tests/parity/`
- **Architecture decisions** → `docs/adr/`
- **Roadmap** → `PLAN.md`
- **Task backlog** → `TODO.md`

## 5. Decisions that must not be silently reversed

These are load-bearing architectural commitments. To change any, open an ADR
and get sign-off from two maintainers.

1. **Pivot-and-NSM translation pipeline** (ADR-0001). Direct language pairs
   are not added; all translation routes through NSM.
2. **Tri-modal architecture** (ADR-0002). Spoken, signed, and tactile are
   first-class; no modality is "translation of" another.
3. **On-device inference only after bootstrap** (ADR-0003). No runtime cloud
   dependency is allowed.
4. **Deterministic failover for every neural component** (ADR-0004). A neural
   component without a parity-tested fallback cannot ship.
5. **Analytic/agglutinative core.** No fusional or polysynthetic core grammar.

## 6. Runbooks

### 6.1 Release a new version

1. Update `CHANGELOG.md` and bump version in `pyproject.toml` and `android/app/build.gradle.kts`.
2. Run `./scripts/verify_all.sh` — must pass on all platforms.
3. Tag `vX.Y.Z`; CI builds desktop wheels and Android APK.
4. Publish release notes; link to parity test results.
5. Announce in community channels.

### 6.2 Rotate a secret

1. Update the GitHub secret.
2. If a model token: revoke old token on Hugging Face, regenerate.
3. If Android keystore: **do not rotate silently** — play store continuity depends on it; coordinate with store listing.

### 6.3 If CI is broken and you're taking over

1. Run `./scripts/verify_all.sh` locally to reproduce.
2. Check whether failures are in `tests/parity/` (likely a model drift) or `tests/unit/` (likely a code change).
3. Parity failures: re-run with `OMNILINGUA_STRICT_PARITY=1` and inspect `tests/parity/reports/`.
4. If a model manifest hash mismatches, open an issue tagged `model-integrity`.

## 7. Known debt

- Tactile realizer is rule-based; no trained model exists yet (see TODO.md `TACTILE-*`).
- Low-resource language coverage in the pivot translator is limited to the
  languages with available parallel corpora; the synthetic data pipeline is
  specified but not yet trained.
- Desktop signing avatar performance on older GPUs is untested.

## 8. Handover checklist

Before declaring the handover complete:

- [ ] All secrets are stored in the org, not in personal accounts.
- [ ] At least two people/agents have admin on the repo, model host, and store listings.
- [ ] This document has been read and updated by the inheritor.
- [ ] A test release was performed end-to-end by the inheritor.
- [ ] All open issues have an `owner:` label or are in `TODO.md`.
```

## AGENT.md

```markdown
# AGENT.md — Instructions for AI Agents Operating on This Repository

> **Audience:** Any AI agent (LLM-based coding assistant, autonomous agent,
> CI bot) that reads, modifies, or reviews this repository.
>
> **Rule zero:** If you are an agent and you are about to make a change that
> affects the language spec (`language/`), the parity contracts
> (`tests/parity/`), or the failover logic (`engine/*/reliability/`), stop and
> follow § 4 (High-Risk Changes) before proceeding.

---

## 1. What kind of project this is

This is a **language + engine + two applications** project. It is unusual in
that the "product" is partly a specification (the conlang) and partly
software. Agents must understand that **the specification is code**: a change
to `language/primes.yaml` changes every downstream renderer, every test, and
every model's training target. Treat language files as APIs.

## 2. Ground truth priority

When documents conflict, trust in this order:

1. **Schema and data files** (`language/schema.sql`, `language/*.yaml`) — the machine-readable truth.
2. **Tests** (`tests/`) — executable truth.
3. **ADRs** (`docs/adr/`) — the *why* behind design decisions.
4. **ARCHITECTURE.md / LANGUAGE_SPEC.md** — human-readable truth; may lag.
5. **README / HANDOVER / PLAN / TODO** — orientation, may lag.

If you find a conflict, **do not silently resolve it**. Open an issue tagged
`doc-drift` and, if you can, fix the lower-priority document.

## 3. Standard agent workflow

Every agent change follows this loop:

1. **Orient**: read `HANDOVER.md` § 5 (load-bearing decisions) and `TODO.md`.
2. **Claim**: find or create an issue. Add the label `agent-working` and a
   comment with your identity and intended scope. Do not work on unclaimed
   tasks.
3. **Branch**: `agent/<short-id>/<slug>` (e.g., `agent/claude-4/nsm-validator-tests`).
4. **Change small**: one logical change per PR. Do not bundle fixes.
5. **Test locally**: `./scripts/verify_all.sh` must pass. For model changes,
   run parity suites with `OMNILINGUA_STRICT_PARITY=1`.
6. **Document**: update the relevant doc *in the same PR*. If you changed a
   language file, update `LANGUAGE_SPEC.md` and add a changelog entry.
7. **PR**: use the template. Tag `agent-authored`. Describe *what*, *why*, and
   *how you verified*.
8. **Wait for human review** for anything in § 4. Agents cannot self-merge
   high-risk changes.

## 4. High-risk changes (require human sign-off)

The following changes **must** be reviewed by a human maintainer before merge.
Agents may prepare the change but must not merge it.

| Area | Examples | Why |
|---|---|---|
| **Language spec** | Adding/removing NSM primes, changing morphosyntax, changing click inventory | Cascades to every component and every model |
| **Parity contracts** | Changing fallback behavior, thresholds, or coverage guarantees | Defines reliability guarantees users depend on |
| **Failover logic** | New triggers, changed recovery FSM, watchdog timing | Safety-critical; must be audited |
| **Model manifests** | Publishing new model versions, changing hashes | Supply-chain integrity |
| **Secrets / CI** | Any change to `.github/workflows/` or secret usage | Security-sensitive |
| **License** | Any change | Legal |

Everything else (tests, docs, refactors, UI, tooling) is normal-risk and may
be merged after standard review.

## 5. Things agents must never do

- **Never** commit model binaries directly. Use the manifest + download script.
- **Never** hardcode credentials. If a secret is needed, request it via an
  issue and let a human provision it.
- **Never** disable a test to make CI pass. Fix the test or mark it
  `@pytest.mark.xfail(reason=...)` with an issue link.
- **Never** change a parity threshold without also changing the test data and
  updating `RELIABILITY.md`.
- **Never** edit `language/schema.sql` without a matching migration in
  `language/migrations/`.
- **Never** touch `HANDOVER.md` § 5 without an ADR.
- **Never** assume the previous conversation state. If context is missing,
  re-read this file and `HANDOVER.md`.

## 6. How to run the project

```bash
./scripts/bootstrap.sh              # first time only
./scripts/verify_all.sh             # all validators + tests
./tools/cli --help                  # CLI surface
python -m desktop.app               # desktop
cd android && ./gradlew :app:test   # android unit tests
```

## 7. Where to look for context

| Question | File |
|---|---|
| What is this project? | `README.md` |
| What's the current state? | `HANDOVER.md` § 1 |
| What's the plan? | `PLAN.md` |
| What's next? | `TODO.md` |
| How does the language work? | `docs/LANGUAGE_SPEC.md` |
| How does the system work? | `docs/ARCHITECTURE.md` |
| How do models work? | `docs/AI_MODELS.md` |
| How does failover work? | `docs/RELIABILITY.md` |
| How is data shaped? | `docs/DATA_FORMATS.md` |
| Why was decision X made? | `docs/adr/` |

## 8. Reporting

Agents should post a summary in the issue at three points: after claiming,
after opening the PR, and after merge (or abandonment). The summary must
include: what changed, what you verified, what you did **not** verify, and any
follow-up issues you created. This is the audit trail.

## 9. If you are unsure

Open an issue tagged `agent-question`. Do not proceed on ambiguous high-risk
changes. A blocked agent is far cheaper than a broken language spec.
```

## PLAN.md

```markdown
# PLAN — Roadmap and Milestones

> **Horizon:** 18 months. Re-baselined quarterly. Each milestone has an exit
> criterion that is **testable**, not aspirational.

---

## Phase 0 — Foundation (weeks 1–6)  ·  **status: in progress**

**Goal:** Freeze the language spec v1.0 and the engine interfaces, so
downstream work has a stable target.

| Deliverable | Exit criterion |
|---|---|
| `language/primes.yaml` (65 primes + combinators) | Passes `tools/validate_primes.py`; reviewed by a linguist |
| `language/phonology.yaml` (incl. 15 click phonemes) | Round-trips through `engine/python/phonology.py` |
| `language/schema.sql` + seed data | `sqlite3 language/omnilingua.db < schema.sql` succeeds |
| Engine interface stubs (Python + Kotlin) | Both compile; contract tests pass |
| ADR-0001 … ADR-0004 | Merged with two maintainer sign-offs |

## Phase 1 — Deterministic Engine (weeks 7–14)

**Goal:** A fully working translation pipeline using **only deterministic
components**. No neural models yet. This establishes the parity baseline.

| Deliverable | Exit criterion |
|---|---|
| Rule-based NSM decomposer (Tier A) | ≥80% exact-prime coverage on the seed corpus |
| Deterministic NSM realizer | Round-trips the seed corpus with ≥95% semantic equivalence |
| Phrasebook pivot translator (5 languages) | 500 high-frequency constructions translate correctly |
| Deterministic TTS (eSpeak NG) + click/hum assets | Audio output is phoneme-valid for the full test set |
| Procedural signing (Animgen/CWASA) | 100 HamNoSys-annotated signs render correctly |
| Tactile realizer (rule-based) | 50 reciprocal constructions produce valid protocol output |
| Full offline desktop app (deterministic only) | Runs in airplane mode; all UI flows work |

**Why this phase matters:** It produces the **fallback paths** that later
neural components must be proven equivalent to. Without this, failover is
untestable.

## Phase 2 — Neural Components with Parity (weeks 15–24)

**Goal:** Add each neural component behind the symbolic shield, with a
passing parity suite against its Phase 1 counterpart.

| Deliverable | Exit criterion |
|---|---|
| NSM decomposer Tier B (distilled student) | Parity suite: ≥60% coverage, 100% validity |
| NSM decomposer Tier C (fine-tuned 8B) | Outperforms Tier B on 200-sample adequacy eval |
| Pivot translator (MobileNMT-style) + LoRA adapters (10 languages) | BLEU ≥ 20 on held-out; INT8 fits memory budget |
| Neural TTS (NeuTTS-2E-style) | MOS ≥ 3.5; click accuracy ≥ 99%; hum contour accuracy ≥ 90% |
| Neural sign diffusion model | Visual realism rating ≥ 3/5 on 50 test signs; falls back for unseen |
| ASR (Whisper base int8) | WER ≤ 15% on conlang audio test set |
| Symbolic shield + watchdog + recovery FSM | Fault-injection suite: 100% failover trigger rate |

## Phase 3 — Mobile Parity (weeks 25–32)

**Goal:** Ship the Android app with the same capabilities and guarantees as
desktop, offline.

| Deliverable | Exit criterion |
|---|---|
| Kotlin port of engine + reliability layer | Cross-platform parity test: same inputs → same outputs |
| ML Kit + Argos-equivalent offline translation | All Phase 1 phrasebook + Phase 2 neural paths work on device |
| Android TTS + click/hum assets | Same phoneme-validity test passes on-device |
| WebView CWASA avatar | All signs render at ≥15 fps on mid-tier device |
| Bootstrap wizard (download only chosen languages) | First-run completes offline-ready in ≤5 min on Wi-Fi |
| Haptics for tactile output | Protocol-display parity on supported devices |

## Phase 4 — Expansion and Community (weeks 33–52)

**Goal:** Broaden language coverage, complete documentation, open for
community contribution, and publish the language spec v1.0.

| Deliverable | Exit criterion |
|---|---|
| 30-language pivot coverage | Parallel corpora available for all; adapters trained |
| Synthetic data pipeline for low-resource | Augmentation improves BLEU on 3 held-out low-resource languages |
| Public spec v1.0 + learnable curriculum | Pilot cohort of 20 learners completes a 10-lesson course |
| Full documentation tree | `docs/` passes link check; every ADR has a status |
| Contribution pipeline (human + agent) | 5 external contributions merged using the documented workflow |

---

## Non-goals (explicitly out of scope)

- Becoming a full replacement for natural languages. This is an auxiliary
  interlingua, not a universal second language.
- Runtime cloud inference. All neural paths are on-device after bootstrap.
- Fusional or polysynthetic core grammar. The analytic/agglutinative core is
  a load-bearing decision (ADR-0001).
- Tactile neural production model until an annotated corpus exists (see
  `TACTILE-RESEARCH` in TODO.md).

---

## Dependencies between phases

```
Phase 0 ──► Phase 1 ──► Phase 2 ──► Phase 3
                     ╲
                      ╲──► Phase 4 (expansion can begin after Phase 1
                                   for language coverage work)
```

Phase 2 **cannot** begin until Phase 1's deterministic counterparts are
complete, because Phase 2's exit criteria are parity against Phase 1.
```

## CONTRIBUTING.md

```markdown
# Contributing to OmniLingua

Humans and AI agents are both welcome. Both follow the same review process.
Agents have additional requirements in [AGENT.md](AGENT.md).

---

## Before you start

- Read [README.md](README.md) for orientation.
- Read [HANDOVER.md](HANDOVER.md) § 5 for load-bearing decisions.
- Check [TODO.md](TODO.md) for unclaimed work.
- Skim [docs/ARCHITECTURE.md](docs/ARCHITECTURE.md) — you need the map.

## Development setup

```bash
git clone https://github.com/<org>/omnilingua.git
cd omnilingua
./scripts/bootstrap.sh
```

`bootstrap.sh` is idempotent. It installs Python deps, seeds the SQLite
language DB, downloads small dev-time model stubs (not the full model stack),
and sets up git hooks that run validators on commit.

If you prefer to set up manually, see [docs/DEVELOPMENT.md](docs/DEVELOPMENT.md).

## Finding something to work on

- Issues labeled `good first issue` are scoped for new contributors.
- Issues labeled `agent-friendly` are scoped for AI agents.
- Everything in [TODO.md](TODO.md) with a blank `Owner` is unclaimed.
- **Claim before you work.** Comment on the issue or add your name to TODO.md
  in the same PR. This prevents duplicate effort.

## The contribution loop

1. **Issue first** for non-trivial changes. Bug fixes and doc improvements
   can go straight to PR.
2. **Branch**: `feat/<slug>`, `fix/<slug>`, or `agent/<id>/<slug>`.
3. **Change small**: one logical change per PR.
4. **Test**: `./scripts/verify_all.sh` must pass locally.
5. **Document**: update the relevant docs in the same PR. If you changed a
   language file, update `docs/LANGUAGE_SPEC.md` and `CHANGELOG.md`.
6. **PR**: fill out the template. Include what/why/how-verified.
7. **Review**: a maintainer reviews. High-risk changes (see
   [AGENT.md](AGENT.md) § 4) require two maintainers.

## What to contribute

| Type | Welcome? | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| Bug fixes | Yes | Include a regression test |
| New tests | Yes | Especially parity tests |
| Documentation | Yes | Keep it factual; link to sources |
| New languages in the pivot | Yes | Requires parallel corpus and a LoRA adapter |
| New models | Discuss first | Open an issue; models affect reliability |
| Language spec changes | ADR required | See below |
| UI changes | Yes | Screenshots in PR |
| Performance work | Yes | Include benchmarks |

## Language spec changes

Any change to `language/` is high-risk because it cascades everywhere.
The process:

1. Open an issue describing the change and its rationale.
2. Write an ADR in `docs/adr/` using the template.
3. Get sign-off from two maintainers.
4. Make the change, update `LANGUAGE_SPEC.md`, add a CHANGELOG entry.
5. Run `./scripts/verify_all.sh` and all parity suites with
   `OMNILINGUA_STRICT_PARITY=1`.

## Code style

- **Python**: PEP 8, `ruff` for lint, `black` for format, `mypy --strict` for types.
- **Kotlin**: `ktlint`, no wildcard imports, prefer `val` over `var`.
- **YAML/SQL**: 2-space indent; validated by `tools/validate_schemas.py`.

## Commit messages

Conventional Commits: `type(scope): summary`. Types: `feat`, `fix`, `docs`,
`test`, `refactor`, `perf`, `chore`, `ci`, `lang` (for language-file changes).

Example: `lang(primes): add DO-combinator for instrument role`

## Review expectations

- Maintainers respond to PRs within 5 business days.
- Agents: if a PR has no review after 7 days, ping the issue with a status
  comment (do not close and reopen).
- If a change is contested, the decision goes to an ADR.

## Community

- Discord / Matrix: link in pinned issue #1.
- Weekly maintainer sync: time in pinned issue.
- Code of conduct: [CODE_OF_CONDUCT.md](CODE_OF_CONDUCT.md).

## License

By contributing, you agree your contribution is licensed under Apache 2.0.
```

# Code of Conduct

This project adopts the [Contributor Covenant v2.1](https://www.contributor-covenant.org/version/2/1/code_of_conduct/).

**Scope:** all project spaces — repo, issues, PRs, chat, and any agent-mediated
interaction.

**Reporting:** email the maintainers at conduct@<domain>. Reports are
confidential. Maintainers will respond within 5 business days.

**AI agents** are expected to follow the same norms. Agent-generated content
that is abusive, spammy, or misrepresents its authorship will be treated as a
violation attributable to the agent's operator.

## SECURITY.md

```markdown
# Security Policy

## Reporting a vulnerability

Email security@<domain>. Do **not** open a public issue for vulnerabilities.
Acknowledge target: 48 hours. Fix target: 14 days for critical.

## Scope

- The desktop and Android applications.
- The model manifest and download pipeline.
- The CI/CD configuration.

## Model supply-chain integrity

- Model files are referenced by manifest, never committed.
- Each manifest records SHA-256 of every artifact.
- The apps verify the hash before loading a model into memory.
- Publishing a new model version is a high-risk change (see AGENT.md § 4).

## Threat model

See `docs/adr/0005-threat-model.md` (in progress). High-level:
- **Adversary:** supply-chain attacker replacing a model file or a dependency.
- **Mitigation:** hash pinning, SBOM generation, dependency scanning in CI,
  two-maintainer sign-off for manifest changes.
```

---

## docs/ARCHITECTURE.md

```markdown
# Architecture

> **Audience:** developers and agents making structural changes.
> For orientation, see [README.md](../README.md).

---

## 1. Design axioms

1. **The specification is code.** `language/` is the source of truth; apps
   read it, they do not embed copies.
2. **Translation routes through meaning.** Every translation is
   source → pivot → NSM → target. No direct pair models (ADR-0001).
3. **Every neural component has a deterministic twin.** A neural component
   cannot ship without a parity-tested fallback (ADR-0004).
4. **Offline after bootstrap.** No runtime cloud dependency (ADR-0003).
5. **Modalities are parallel, not derived.** Spoken, signed, and tactile are
   first-class renderers of the same NSM structure (ADR-0002).

## 2. Layer diagram

```
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ Frontends                                                    │
│  desktop/ (PySide6)              android/ (Compose)          │
├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│ Reliability (deterministic)                                  │
│  IntentRouter → SymbolicShield → Watchdog → RecoveryFSM      │
│  AuditLog                                                    │
├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│ Engine                                                       │
│  PivotTranslator → NSMDecomposer → NSMRealizer               │
│  (each has neural + deterministic implementations)           │
├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│ Renderers                                                    │
│  SpokenTTS │ SignProducer (SiGML) │ TactileEncoder            │
├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│ Data                                                         │
│  SQLite language DB │ model manifests │ corpora │ audio      │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```

## 3. Data flow for a translation request

```
input(text, source_lang, target_modality)
  │
  ▼
IntentRouter ──► (deterministic, classifies input)
  │
  ▼
PivotTranslator(source → en)
  │   neural: MobileNMT+LoRA
  │   deterministic: phrasebook / template
  ▼
NSMDecomposer(en → NSM structure)
  │   neural: Tier B/C LLM + symbolic validator
  │   deterministic: Tier A template parser
  ▼
NSMRealizer(NSM → conlang surface form)
  │   deterministic: transducer (primary)
  │   neural: small seq2seq (fallback only)
  ▼
Renderer(surface form → modality)
  │   spoken: TTS + click/hum assets
  │   signed: HamNoSys → SiGML → Animgen
  │   tactile: rule-based protocol encoder
  ▼
output(text, audio, sigml, tactile_protocol)
```

Each neural step is wrapped by the symbolic shield. If any step fails
validation, the shield invokes the deterministic twin for that step and the
pipeline continues. The audit log records the failover.

## 4. Component ownership

| Component | Python module | Kotlin module | Parity suite |
|---|---|---|---|
| IntentRouter | `engine/python/reliability/intent_router.py` | `engine/kotlin/reliability/IntentRouter.kt` | `tests/parity/test_intent_router.py` |
| SymbolicShield | `.../symbolic_shield.py` | `.../SymbolicShield.kt` | `tests/parity/test_shield.py` |
| PivotTranslator | `.../engine/pivot_translator.py` | `.../engine/PivotTranslator.kt` | `tests/parity/test_pivot.py` |
| NSMDecomposer | `.../engine/nsm_decomposer.py` | `.../engine/NSMDecomposer.kt` | `tests/parity/test_nsm_decompose.py` |
| NSMRealizer | `.../engine/nsm_realizer.py` | `.../engine/NSMRealizer.kt` | `tests/parity/test_nsm_realize.py` |
| SpokenTTS | `.../renderers/tts.py` | `.../renderers/Tts.kt` | `tests/parity/test_tts.py` |
| SignProducer | `.../renderers/sign.py` | `.../renderers/Sign.kt` | `tests/parity/test_sign.py` |
| TactileEncoder | `.../renderers/tactile.py` | `.../renderers/Tactile.kt` | `tests/parity/test_tactile.py` |

## 5. Adding a new component

1. Define the deterministic implementation first (Phase 1 discipline).
2. Define the parity contract in `tests/parity/`.
3. Add the neural implementation behind the symbolic shield.
4. Add a fault-injection test that proves failover works.
5. Add the component to the table in § 4.
6. Update `HANDOVER.md` § 3 if it introduces a new dependency.

## 6. Further reading

- [LANGUAGE_SPEC.md](LANGUAGE_SPEC.md) — the language itself.
- [AI_MODELS.md](AI_MODELS.md) — model stack.
- [RELIABILITY.md](RELIABILITY.md) — failover.

## docs/RELIABILITY.md

```markdown
# Reliability: Deterministic Failover and Self-Healing

> **Audience:** anyone touching `engine/*/reliability/` or
> `tests/parity/`. This document is the contract that those directories
> implement.

---

## 1. The invariant

**Every neural component has a deterministic counterpart with a defined
parity contract. Failover is automatic, deterministic, and auditable.**

A component that violates this invariant cannot ship.

## 2. Execution tiers

| Tier | What | Determinism |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | IntentRouter — classifies, selects lane | 100% |
| 2 | Neural path — handles ambiguous input | Stochastic |
| 3 | Deterministic fallback | 100% |

## 3. Parity contract

A parity contract is a vector, not a scalar. Every component defines:

| Dimension | Meaning | How measured |
|---|---|---|
| Semantic equivalence | Same meaning for in-domain inputs | Back-translation + adequacy rating |
| Functional coverage | % of neural path's input domain handled | Coverage matrix by language/modality |
| Latency ceiling | P95 latency on target hardware | Benchmarks in `tests/bench/` |
| Modality coverage | Output in required modality | Modality-specific acceptance tests |
| Safety invariants | Never violates hard constraints | Runtime monitor + formal spec |

Thresholds are per-component and live in `tests/parity/config.yaml`. Changing
a threshold is a high-risk change.

## 4. Failover triggers (deterministic)

- **Validation failure** — output violates schema / prime inventory / grammar
- **Confidence below threshold** — calibrated score below floor
- **Latency breach** — P95 deadline exceeded
- **Resource exhaustion** — memory/compute/battery below margin
- **Integrity failure** — model hash mismatch or memory corruption
- **Repeated inconsistency** — same input, divergent outputs across runs

Triggers are evaluated by deterministic code, never by the neural model.

## 5. Recovery state machine

```
HEALTHY ──trigger──► DEGRADED ──canary pass──► HEALTHY
   ▲                    │
   │                    │ canary fail
   │                    ▼
   └──── canary pass ── FAILED ◄── rollback ── AUTO_REVERT
```

Recovery requires:
1. Re-instantiate the component.
2. Run the canary set with expected outputs.
3. Promote to active **only if** canary passes.
4. Otherwise remain in fallback and retry with exponential backoff.

## 6. Self-healing mechanisms

- **Watchdog** on a separate thread/core tracks inference deadlines.
- **Auto-revert** to last known-good model on regression.
- **Explicit degraded state** surfaced in UI and logged; never silent.
- **Canary-gated re-entry** prevents flapping.

## 7. Testing requirements

Every component must pass:

- **Fault injection**: disable neural path, corrupt model, inject latency,
  starve resources. Failover must trigger 100% of the time.
- **Parity suite**: frozen inputs with expected deterministic outputs;
  divergence measured and within contract.
- **Chaos tests**: environmental factors, hardware faults, adversarial inputs.
- **Audit trail check**: every failover and recovery event logged with a
  deterministic signature.

`./scripts/verify_all.sh` runs all of the above. `OMNILINGUA_STRICT_PARITY=1`
turns divergences into failures instead of warnings.

## 8. Changing the contract

1. Write an ADR.
2. Update `tests/parity/config.yaml` and `tests/parity/data/`.
3. Update this document.
4. Get two-maintainer sign-off.
5. Run strict parity on CI before merge.
```

## docs/OFFLINE.md

```markdown
# Offline Strategy

> **Guarantee:** Both apps run fully offline after a one-time bootstrap.
> No runtime cloud dependency. See ADR-0003.

---

## 1. Bootstrap

First launch downloads:
- Selected source-language ML Kit models (Android) or Argos packs (desktop), ~30 MB each.
- Offline TTS voice data if not already on device.

Everything else — language DB, conlang audio assets, signing avatar WebView,
model manifests and weights for the conlang pipeline — is **bundled in the
installer/APK**.

The bootstrap is a **setup step**, not a runtime dependency. After it, the app
shows "Offline Ready" and operates in airplane mode.

## 2. Per-platform replacements

| Function | Cloud (rejected) | Offline replacement |
|---|---|---|
| Pivot translation | Google Cloud Translation | ML Kit (Android) / Argos (Python) |
| NSM decomposition | Cloud LLM | Local small LLM + rule-based |
| TTS | Cloud TTS | Android TTS / eSpeak NG / Piper |
| Signing avatar | JASigning server | CWASA client-side Animgen in WebView |
| Clicks/hum audio | Streamed | Bundled assets |

## 3. Verification

`tests/offline/` runs the full pipeline with the network interface stubbed to
raise on any call. The test suite must pass with zero network access.

## 4. Fallback when offline assets are missing

If a bootstrap asset is missing (e.g., user declined a language model):
- The IntentRouter detects the missing capability.
- The app shows an explicit **degraded-mode notice** identifying what is
  unavailable.
- The deterministic fallback (phrasebook for that language) is used.
- The user is offered a retry of the bootstrap for that asset.

No silent degradation. See `docs/RELIABILITY.md` § 6.
```

## docs/DEVELOPMENT.md

```markdown
# Development Setup

## Prerequisites

- Python 3.11+
- JDK 17 + Android SDK (for Android)
- `git`, `sqlite3`, `ffmpeg` (for audio asset processing)
- ~2 GB free disk (dev-time model stubs)

## One-shot setup

```bash
./scripts/bootstrap.sh
```

This will:
1. Create a Python venv in `.venv/`.
2. Install Python deps from `pyproject.toml`.
3. Seed `language/omnilingua.db` from `language/schema.sql` + data files.
4. Download dev-time model stubs to `models/dev-stubs/` (small, not the full stack).
5. Install git hooks that run `ruff`, `mypy`, and schema validators on commit.
6. Install Android SDK components if `ANDROID_HOME` is set.

## Daily commands

```bash
./scripts/verify_all.sh            # lint + type-check + tests + parity + offline
python -m desktop.app              # desktop app
python -m pytest tests/unit -q     # fast unit tests only
cd android && ./gradlew :app:test  # Android unit tests
./tools/cli --help                 # CLI surface
```

## Environment variables

| Var | Purpose | Default |
|---|---|---|
| `OMNILINGUA_HOME` | Data dir for DB and models | repo root |
| `OMNILINGUA_STRICT_PARITY` | Treat parity divergence as failure | `0` |
| `OMNILINGUA_DEV_MODELS` | Use dev stubs instead of full models | `1` |

## Troubleshooting

- **`bootstrap.sh` fails on SQLite seed**: delete `language/omnilingua.db` and re-run.
- **Android build fails on JDK**: ensure `JAVA_HOME` points at JDK 17.
- **Parity tests fail after pulling**: re-run `bootstrap.sh` — data files may have changed.
```

## docs/DATA_FORMATS.md

```markdown
# Data Formats

## SQLite schema

The canonical schema is `language/schema.sql`. Migrations live in
`language/migrations/` and are applied by `tools/migrate.py`.

### Tables

| Table | Purpose | Key columns |
|---|---|---|
| `primes` | NSM primes + combinators | `id`, `name`, `gloss`, `combinator` |
| `lexemes` | Conventionalized roots | `id`, `phon_form`, `click`, `tone` |
| `senses` | Meanings attached to lexemes | `id`, `lexeme_id`, `prime_decomp` |
| `signs` | HamNoSys annotations | `id`, `lexeme_id`, `hamnosys`, `nonmanual` |
| `tactile` | Protactile constructions | `id`, `sign_id`, `protocol_json` |
| `parity_gold` | Frozen expected outputs | `id`, `component`, `input_hash`, `output_json` |

### Migrations

Never edit `schema.sql` without a migration. Rules:

1. Migrations are numbered: `0001_init.sql`, `0002_add_signs.sql`.
2. Each migration is forward-only and idempotent where possible.
3. `tools/migrate.py` applies pending migrations in order and records them in
   `schema_migrations`.

## YAML files

All YAML files under `language/` are validated by `tools/validate_schemas.py`
against JSON Schema files in `language/schemas/`. A file that fails
validation blocks CI.

## JSON output schemas

Engine outputs use JSON with stable schemas:

- `NSMStructure`: `{ "primes": [...], "combinators": [...] }`
- `ConlangSurface`: `{ "phonemes": [...], "clitics": [...], "mood": "..." }`
- `SigML`: XML per SiGML spec.
- `TactileProtocol`: `{ "conveyer_hand": "...", "receiver_location": "...", "movement": "...", "contact": "..." }`

Schemas live in `engine/schemas/` and are versioned.

## Change discipline

Any change to a schema requires:
1. A migration (for SQLite).
2. A JSON Schema update.
3. A parity gold update if it changes outputs.
4. A CHANGELOG entry.
```

## docs/GLOSSARY.md

```markdown
# Glossary

## Project terms

- **NSM** — Natural Semantic Metalanguage. The 65-prime semantic core.
- **Prime** — An irreducible semantic unit (e.g., SOMEONE, GOOD, WANT).
- **Combinator** — A grammatical relation between primes (predicate, argument, modifier).
- **Pivot** — The intermediate natural language (English) used between source and NSM.
- **Conlang** — The constructed language of this project.
- **Tri-modal** — Spoken, signed, tactile as first-class expression channels.
- **Parity contract** — The vector-valued equivalence guarantee for a fallback.
- **Symbolic shield** — The deterministic validator around a neural component.
- **Recovery FSM** — The state machine managing failover and re-entry.
- **Bootstrap** — The one-time download step; not a runtime dependency.

## Typology terms

- **Agglutinative** — Words built from discrete affixes, one meaning each.
- **Analytic / isolating** — Little inflection; grammar via word order and free words.
- **Fusional** — Multiple grammatical categories fused into one morpheme.
- **Polysynthetic** — Many morphemes per word, including incorporated nouns.
- **Ergative** — Aligns intransitive subject with transitive object.
- **Accusative** — Aligns transitive and intransitive subjects together.
- **Sprachbund** — Area where unrelated languages converge on shared features.

## Standards

- **HamNoSys** — Hamburg Notation System for sign language.
- **SiGML** — XML format for sign language gesture markup.
- **CWASA** — Client-side Web Avatar System for Animgen.
- **SSML** — Speech Synthesis Markup Language.
```

## docs/adr/0004-deterministic-failover.md

```markdown
# ADR-0004: Deterministic Failover for Every Neural Component

- **Status:** Accepted
- **Date:** YYYY-MM-DD
- **Deciders:** @maintainer, @backup

## Context

The project uses neural models for translation, NSM decomposition, TTS, sign
production, and ASR. Neural components can fail silently, produce invalid
output, or become unavailable offline. Without a deterministic fallback, the
system has no reliability guarantee.

## Decision

Every neural component must have a deterministic counterpart with a defined
parity contract and automatic failover on auditable triggers. A component
without a passing parity suite cannot ship. Failover triggers are evaluated by
deterministic code, never by the neural model. Recovery is canary-gated.

## Consequences

- Phase 1 (deterministic engine) must complete before Phase 2 (neural
  components), because Phase 2's exit criteria are parity against Phase 1.
- Every component has two implementations and two test suites.
- Model updates require re-running parity suites before release.
- The system degrades gracefully and audibly; it never fails silently.

## Alternatives considered

- **Fail-open with error messages**: rejected — the app must remain useful
  offline, not just report failure.
- **Single neural path with no fallback**: rejected — violates the offline
  guarantee and the reliability invariant.
- **Cloud fallback**: rejected — violates ADR-0003.
```
